title: Carmen
facts: Carmen premiered at the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 3 March 1875, and its broken conventions shocked its first audiences.
Bizet died suddenly of heart disease the day after the 33rd performance, at 36. He never knew Carmen would conquer the world.
The Habanera is based on “El arreglito” by Sebastián Yradier. Bizet thought it was a folk tune; when he found out, he credited Yradier in the score.
Bizet also rewrote the words of Carmen’s Habanera himself.
Bizet was reportedly contemptuous of the Toreador Song: “Well, they asked for ordure, and they’ve got it.”
Micaëla brings Don José a letter and a kiss from his mother. The librettists added her to soften the story for the family theatre.
The Opéra-Comique’s co-director, de Leuven, opposed staging such a risqué story in what he considered a family theatre.
At the premiere, the only applause in Act III was for Micaëla’s aria, as the audience grew more and more uneasy.
The next day’s reviews ranged from disappointment to outrage. One critic called Galli-Marié’s Carmen “the very incarnation of vice”.
After the premiere Bizet reportedly said: “Don’t you see that all these bourgeois have not understood a wretched word of the work I have written for them?”
Bizet, as reported by Benjamin Godard (via Wikipedia)
Tchaikovsky wrote to his patron Nadezhda von Meck: “Carmen is a masterpiece in every sense of the word.”
Tchaikovsky, letter to Nadezhda von Meck (via Wikipedia)
Brahms reportedly saw Carmen twenty times and said he would have “gone to the ends of the earth to embrace Bizet”.
Carmen first played at the Metropolitan Opera on 9 January 1884, to mixed reviews.
Enrico Caruso sang José on the Met tour in San Francisco on 17 April 1906. Two hours later the great earthquake hit, and the singers fled the Palace Hotel.
Bizet was still revising Carmen when he died, and later changes (like Guiraud’s recitatives) mean there is still no definitive edition.
Before the last scene, a chorus and procession announce the toreador Escamillo: “Vivat, vivat le Toréro!”
